stem: A German insurer is building a claims summarizer that calls Claude through its cloud provider's managed model service. The data protection officer has ruled that claim text may be processed only inside the EU, and the prototype currently uses the provider's global endpoint for availability. Which change satisfies the requirement?

options.text: Switch to the provider's EU regional endpoint, which guarantees that requests are routed and processed in that region
options.why: Correct. Residency is about where inference runs, and a regional endpoint is the control that pins processing to the required geography.

options.text: Keep the global endpoint and encrypt the claim text with a customer-managed key before every single request is sent
options.why: Encryption protects confidentiality in transit and at rest, but the model still has to process the text wherever the global endpoint routes it.

options.text: Keep the global endpoint and shorten the retention period on the application logs that hold claim text
options.why: Retention controls how long data is kept, a different requirement dimension from where the data is processed.

options.text: Add a system prompt instruction stating that Claude must process each claim within EU jurisdiction only
options.why: A prompt cannot change request routing; the model has no say in which data center serves the call.

explanation: The cue is 'processed only inside the EU', a residency requirement. Global endpoints route dynamically for availability, which is exactly what residency forbids, while a regional endpoint guarantees the processing location. Encryption is the tempting distractor, but it changes who can read the data, not where inference happens.
cue: may be processed only inside the EU

stem: A brokerage's support assistant drafts replies that go straight to retail customers. Compliance requires that account numbers are stripped from every outgoing reply with no exceptions, and a junior engineer proposes adding a redaction instruction to the system prompt. Which design meets the requirement?

options.text: Expand the system prompt with examples of every account-number format and a firm instruction to redact them
options.why: More examples improve compliance rates, but a prompt is still a request the model can miss, so it cannot meet a no-exceptions rule.

options.text: Return each reply through a structured output schema that deliberately has no field for account numbers
options.why: A schema controls which fields exist, not what text appears inside the reply field, so a number can still be written into it.

options.text: Send every draft to a second Claude call that reviews it and removes any account numbers it finds
options.why: A second model pass lowers the miss rate but is still probabilistic, so it cannot guarantee zero leaks.

options.text: Run a deterministic redaction filter in code on every reply before delivery, whatever the model produced
options.why: Correct. Code that runs on every reply enforces the rule regardless of model behaviour, which is what 'no exceptions' demands.

explanation: 'With no exceptions' turns this into a must-requirement, and only a deterministic control placed in the delivery path can guarantee it. The second-model reviewer is the most tempting distractor because it feels like defence in depth, but it can be wrong in the same way the first call can. Prompt and model layers may still help, as long as the code filter is the enforcement point.

stem: An HR tool brief says Claude should draft a personalised onboarding email from each new hire's role and start date. The same brief says the first token of each draft must appear within one second even when 200 hires start on the same day. How should an analyst classify these two statements?

options.text: Both are infrastructure requirements, because both describe how the system behaves under real operating conditions
options.why: Drafting the email is the capability being built, so calling it infrastructure confuses what the system does with the envelope it runs in.

options.text: Both are functional requirements, because neither one names a vendor, a hosting region or a platform
options.why: Infrastructure requirements are not defined by naming a vendor; a latency target under concurrent load is non-functional either way.

options.text: Drafting the email is functional; the one-second first token across 200 concurrent hires is infrastructure
options.why: Correct. One statement describes behaviour, the other a latency and throughput envelope that shapes configuration, not features.

options.text: The latency target is functional, because it directly shapes what the end user experiences in the tool
options.why: Users feel latency, but it is still a quality attribute of how the feature performs rather than a capability of the feature.

explanation: Functional requirements state what the system does; infrastructure requirements state the envelope it must do it within. The cue is a time budget under concurrent load, which is latency plus throughput. The tempting error is treating anything users notice as functional.
cue: the first token of each draft must appear within one second even when 200 hires start on the same day

stem: A general counsel asks for 'real-time contract risk scoring' on incoming supplier contracts. In discovery you learn the scores are only read at the legal team's Thursday review meeting, and nobody acts on a score between meetings. Which latency requirement should go into the specification?

options.text: Scores for each week's contracts must be ready before the Thursday review starts, with no interactive latency target
options.why: Correct. The requirement comes from how the output is consumed, and the only consumer reads it once a week at a fixed time.

options.text: Time to first token must stay under 500 milliseconds so that scores begin to appear as soon as a contract arrives
options.why: This optimizes the sponsor's adjective; nobody is watching a screen when a contract arrives, so a streaming target buys nothing.

options.text: End-to-end scoring must finish within two seconds at the 95th percentile for every contract that is uploaded
options.why: A tight percentile target constrains tier and architecture choices to serve a waiting user who does not exist in this process.

options.text: Scores must be pushed to the legal team's dashboard over a persistent connection the moment they are ready
options.why: Push delivery solves a freshness problem the scenario does not have, adding moving parts for a weekly reader.

explanation: Stakeholder adjectives are not specifications; usage is. The cue is that scores are only read at a weekly meeting, so the real requirement is a deadline, not a latency budget. The distractors all turn 'real-time' into a number without asking who is waiting.
cue: only read at the legal team's Thursday review meeting

stem: A benefits assistant returns accurate answers, but at the Monday peak about 15% of calls fail with 429 errors. Every request sends the same 80-page benefits handbook ahead of a short user question, and the usage chart shows input tokens per minute at the limit while requests per minute stay well below it. Which change most directly raises usable throughput?

options.text: Cache the repeated handbook prefix, since cached input reads do not count toward the input-token rate limit on most models
options.why: Correct. Cache reads are excluded from ITPM on most current models, so a high hit rate multiplies effective input volume without a limit increase.

options.text: Raise max_tokens on each request so that every answer completes in one call and users send fewer follow-up questions
options.why: max_tokens caps output and does not factor into OTPM, and the binding limit here is input tokens, so it changes nothing.

options.text: Increase the SDK retry count so that failed calls are retried several more times before the error is shown to users
options.why: Retries help a transient burst, but the input budget is exhausted every peak, so extra retries mostly add load and delay.

options.text: Move to the most capable model tier so each answer is more complete and users ask fewer clarifying follow-up questions
options.why: The content is already fine; a larger tier does not shrink the repeated handbook tokens that are exhausting the input limit.

explanation: The cue is the same large handbook sent ahead of every question while ITPM, not RPM, is the binding limit. Prompt caching turns that repeated prefix into cache reads, which do not count toward ITPM on most models. Retries are the tempting answer, but they treat a capacity problem as a transient one.
cue: Every request sends the same 80-page benefits handbook ahead of a short user question

stem: A law firm's discovery assistant lets associates question the same privileged case file across dozens of turns. The firm's contract with Anthropic is a zero data retention arrangement that no workload may step outside, and an engineer wants to avoid paying full price to resend the large file every turn. Which design fits?

options.text: Send the case file inline in each Messages request and put a prompt-caching breakpoint after it to cut repeat cost
options.why: Correct. Inline Messages requests and prompt caching are ZDR-eligible, and caching cuts the cost of the repeated prefix.

options.text: Upload the case file once through the Files API, reference its file ID each turn, and delete it when the matter closes
options.why: The Files API stores files until they are deleted or expire, so it is not ZDR-eligible even with a cleanup step.

options.text: Load the case file into a code execution container once so Claude can search it with code across many turns
options.why: Code execution keeps container data for up to 30 days and is listed as not ZDR-eligible, which breaks the retention rule.

options.text: Pre-process the case file into summaries with a Message Batches job and pass only those summaries into each turn
options.why: Batch jobs are stored for asynchronous processing and are retained for 29 days, so they sit outside a ZDR arrangement.

explanation: The deciding clause is that no workload may step outside zero data retention. Stateful features (Files, code execution containers, Batch) are documented as not ZDR-eligible because they must store data, while inline Messages requests and prompt caching are eligible. The Files API is the tempting choice because deleting the file feels like zero retention, but the file is still stored between turns. [Likely: eligibility lists drift, check the retention page.]
cue: zero data retention arrangement that no workload may step outside

stem: An insurer wants Claude to help onboard new policyholders: read the uploaded ID document, check the name against a sanctions-screening API, and draft a welcome letter. Every applicant goes through the same three steps in the same order, and auditors must be able to trace which step produced each decision. Which architecture fits best?

options.text: A fixed workflow in code: Claude extracts the ID fields, code calls the screening API, then Claude drafts the letter
options.why: Correct. A predefined code path matches a fixed sequence, guarantees the screening call happens, and leaves a step-by-step trace.

options.text: An autonomous agent given ID, screening and letter tools that decides for itself which tool to call next
options.why: Autonomy is useful when the path cannot be known in advance; here it adds variance and makes the audit trail harder to read.

options.text: An orchestrator agent that delegates each applicant's three steps to separate subagents and merges the results
options.why: Orchestration suits work that must be decomposed dynamically; a fixed three-step path gains cost and latency for no benefit.

options.text: A single Claude call with the screening API exposed as a tool, prompted to run the three steps in order
options.why: The model still decides whether and when to call the screening tool, so a mandatory step depends on a prompt rather than code.

explanation: The cue is 'the same three steps in the same order': known steps mean a workflow, not an agent. Anthropic's guidance is to use the simplest system that works and reserve agents for open-ended problems where the steps cannot be predicted. The single call with a tool is the tempting distractor, but it leaves the mandatory sanctions check to the model's discretion.
cue: Every applicant goes through the same three steps in the same order

stem: A freight portal uses Claude to draft quote emails for customers. The surcharge in each quote must match the published rate table by weight band and zone to the cent, and the email must explain the charge in plain language. Where should the surcharge be computed?

options.text: Include the rate table in the system prompt and have Claude look up and state the surcharge while drafting
options.why: Claude usually gets the lookup right, but 'to the cent, every quote' is a guarantee a model cannot give.

options.text: In application code from the rate table, passing the computed amount to Claude to explain in the email
options.why: Correct. Code applies the deterministic rule exactly; Claude does the language work it is suited for.

options.text: In Claude's structured output, using a schema with minimum and maximum bounds on the surcharge field
options.why: Numeric bounds are not supported in structured output schemas, and a value inside a range can still be the wrong amount.

options.text: In a Claude call with extended reasoning enabled so it works through the table step by step before answering
options.why: More reasoning lowers the error rate but does not make a lookup deterministic, so it cannot meet a must-match rule.

explanation: The cue is 'must match the published rate table ... to the cent', a deterministic business rule. A lookup belongs in code, with the model explaining a number it was given. The schema-bounds option is tempting, but structured outputs do not support numeric minimum and maximum, and a range check would not prove the amount right anyway.
cue: must match the published rate table by weight band and zone to the cent

stem: A product owner's requirement for a ticket triage feature reads 'Claude should categorize tickets accurately.' Before design starts, the team needs an acceptance criterion that a release pipeline can check automatically. Which rewrite provides one?

options.text: At least 95% of 500 human-labelled tickets receive the labelled category, beating the current baseline
options.why: Correct. It is specific, measurable on a named set and compared with a baseline, so code can grade it on every release.

options.text: The system prompt tells Claude to categorize carefully, double-check its choice and avoid guessing
options.why: This is an implementation choice, not a criterion; nothing in it can be measured as passed or failed by a pipeline.

options.text: The feature runs on the most capable available model so that categorization quality is maximized
options.why: A model choice is a design decision; it states no threshold, so nobody can tell whether the requirement is met.

options.text: The product owner personally reviews twenty sample categorizations before launch and confirms they look right
options.why: A one-off subjective review on a tiny sample cannot run in a pipeline and does not state what 'right' means.

explanation: Good success criteria are specific, measurable, achievable and relevant, and Anthropic's example replaces 'classify sentiments well' with an F1 target on a held-out set. The cue is that the pipeline must check it automatically, which needs a threshold on labelled data. The prompt and model options describe how to try, not how to verify.
cue: an acceptance criterion that a release pipeline can check automatically

stem: Claude extracts fields from supplier invoices into JSON that a billing service ingests automatically. Many invoices have no purchase-order number, and the requirement says the system must never invent one, because the billing service sends any invoice without a PO to a manual queue. How should the po_number field be specified?

options.text: As a required string field, with a prompt instruction to write N/A whenever the invoice shows no PO number
options.why: A sentinel string is just another PO-shaped value to the billing service, and the instruction to use it is not enforced.

options.text: As a required field typed string or null in a structured-output schema, with code routing null to the manual queue
options.why: Correct. A nullable type gives the model a valid way to say 'absent', and code acts on null deterministically.

options.text: As a required string field with a regex pattern for the PO format, so malformed or invented values fail validation
options.why: A pattern checks shape, not truth; an invented number in the right format passes, and a forced string invites invention.

options.text: As an optional field the model may omit, with the billing service treating a missing key as an extraction error
options.why: This conflates a legitimate absent PO with a failed extraction, so valid invoices land in an error path instead of the queue.

explanation: The cue is 'must never invent one' combined with a downstream consumer. A required string field pressures the model to fill something in, while a nullable field in an enforced schema makes absence a first-class, machine-readable answer that code can route. The regex option is tempting, but format validation cannot detect a plausible fabricated number.

stem: A retail chat assistant gives accurate answers, but full responses take about nine seconds to arrive. Session analytics show shoppers abandon the chat if no text appears within two seconds, and the accuracy eval must not regress. Which two changes address the requirement? Select two.

options.text: Stream the response so that text renders as tokens are generated instead of after the full reply
options.why: Correct. Streaming cuts time to first visible text, which is exactly the abandonment threshold being measured.

options.text: Test a faster model tier against the accuracy eval and switch to it if the eval still passes
options.why: Correct. A faster tier lowers latency, and gating the switch on the eval respects the no-regression constraint.

options.text: Raise the client timeout so that long responses are allowed to complete instead of failing
options.why: Nothing is timing out; a longer timeout lets slow responses finish but shows the shopper nothing sooner.

options.text: Move the requests to the Message Batches API so that they are processed on separate capacity
options.why: Batch is asynchronous with results arriving later, the opposite of what a waiting shopper needs.

options.text: Raise max_tokens so that long answers are never truncated before they reach the shopper
options.why: Truncation is not the complaint, and allowing longer outputs can only make full responses slower.

explanation: The cue is that shoppers leave if no text appears within two seconds, a time-to-first-token requirement with a person waiting. Streaming improves perceived responsiveness and a faster tier cuts latency, provided the accuracy eval still passes. The timeout option is tempting because the responses are slow, but it changes when a call fails, not when text appears.
cue: abandon the chat if no text appears within two seconds

stem: A telecom wants a Claude agent that can issue account credits to cut call-handling time. The business rules state that any credit above $200 requires a supervisor's approval before it is applied, and every credit decision must be reconstructable for quarterly audits. Which two design elements meet these requirements? Select two.

options.text: Code in the credit tool path that holds any credit above $200 in a supervisor queue until it is approved
options.why: Correct. The threshold check runs outside the model, so the approval step happens whatever the agent decides.

options.text: An append-only log of each credit tool call with its inputs, the decision taken and the approver's identity
options.why: Correct. Recording every call and approval outside the model is what makes each decision reconstructable later.

options.text: A system prompt rule telling the agent to ask a supervisor before issuing any credit above $200
options.why: The agent will usually comply, but a prompt is a request, so the approval requirement is not enforced.

options.text: A more capable model tier so the agent judges more reliably which credits need a supervisor
options.why: Better judgement reduces mistakes but cannot guarantee a mandatory approval step for every qualifying credit.

options.text: An instruction for the agent to explain its reasoning to the customer so each decision is documented
options.why: Customer-facing explanations are not an audit record; they are unstructured, can be wrong and are not stored for review.

explanation: Both requirements are musts: approval before money moves, and decisions reconstructable later. Each needs an enforced component in code: a gate on the tool path and a durable log. The system prompt rule is the tempting distractor because it usually works, but a requirement phrased as 'requires' needs a control, not a request.
cue: any credit above $200 requires a supervisor's approval before it is applied

stem: A benefits-enrollment assistant was prototyped on the cheapest, fastest model tier, which the product team prefers for cost. Legal has since confirmed that inference must run only on US infrastructure, and the cheapest tier does not support the US-only inference setting on the platform the team uses. How should the team resolve the conflict?

options.text: Treat US-only inference as a hard filter, then choose the cheapest tier that supports it and still passes the eval
options.why: Correct. Hard constraints remove options first; cost and speed preferences then rank the tiers that survive.

options.text: Keep the cheapest tier and send its requests through an API gateway hosted in a US cloud region
options.why: The gateway's location says nothing about where the model provider runs inference, so the requirement is not met.

options.text: Keep the cheapest tier and set the workspace default geography to US so that every request from the app inherits that setting
options.why: A workspace default cannot make a tier that lacks US-only support run there; the tier still cannot meet the rule.

options.text: Keep the cheapest tier and record the residency gap as an accepted risk until the tier gains support
options.why: Legal has stated a must; a confirmed legal requirement is not a risk the delivery team can choose to accept.

explanation: The cue is that legal says inference 'must run only on US infrastructure', a hard constraint that outranks the cost preference. Resolve conflicts by filtering on hard constraints and ranking on preferences, accepting the higher price if needed. The workspace-default option is tempting because it is a real enforcement lever, but it cannot add support to a model that lacks it. [Likely: per-model geo support drifts.]
cue: inference must run only on US infrastructure
author: agent:q-requirements-lifecycle

stem: Finance has approved a summarization feature with a ceiling of $3,000 a month and wants usage to stop rather than overrun if the ceiling is reached. The feature runs in its own workspace on the Claude API. Which control satisfies this requirement?

options.text: A spend limit on the feature's workspace, so requests return an error once that limit is reached
options.why: Correct. A workspace spend limit is enforced by the platform, so usage stops at the ceiling instead of overrunning.

options.text: A system prompt instruction asking Claude to keep every summary short so monthly spend stays low
options.why: Shorter outputs lower the average cost, but nothing stops spending once the ceiling is crossed.

options.text: A monthly cost report from the usage export, reviewed by finance at each month-end close
options.why: A report is detective, not preventive; the overrun has already happened by the time anyone reads it.

options.text: A lower max_tokens value on each request so that every individual summary costs less to make
options.why: This caps the cost of one response, not the monthly total, which still grows with request volume.

explanation: The cue is 'stop rather than overrun', which asks for an enforced ceiling. Workspace spend limits make requests fail once reached, so the requirement maps to configuration rather than to prompt or token tuning. Lowering max_tokens is tempting because it does reduce cost, but it bounds each call, not the month.
cue: wants usage to stop rather than overrun

stem: A hospital operations director asks for an assistant that summarizes discharge notes and says only that it 'must be secure and compliant'. Before any design work, you need to turn that phrase into requirements an architect can act on. Which two clarifying questions do that most directly? Select two.

options.text: Which regulation governs these notes, and where may the data be processed?
options.why: Correct. It names the regime and the residency limit, which decide endpoints, regions and eligible features.

options.text: May the AI vendor store prompts or outputs, and if so for how long?
options.why: Correct. The answer sets the retention requirement, which rules features in or out of the design.

options.text: Which model tier does the director prefer for summarization quality?
options.why: Tier preference is a quality and cost question; it does not decode what 'secure and compliant' requires.

options.text: Should the system prompt remind Claude that the data is confidential?
options.why: This jumps to a prompt-level tactic, which is not a requirement and cannot enforce any compliance rule.

options.text: What reading level and tone should the discharge summaries use?
options.why: Tone is a legitimate functional detail, but it says nothing about security or compliance obligations.

explanation: 'Secure and compliant' hides data-class, residency and retention requirements, and you decode an adjective by asking which regulation, which data and where it may go. Those answers decide regions, endpoints and which stateful features are allowed. The system-prompt question is tempting because it sounds security-minded, but it is a tactic, not a requirement.
author: agent:q-requirements-lifecycle
